planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained soil amended with compost, setting the crown about an inch below the surface.

directions: Registered in 2015 by James Gossard, this tetraploid daylily carries intense orange petals surrounding a red-orange eyezone and a yellow-orange throat, with an unusual, slightly twisted petal form. Tall, dormant-foliage scapes rise to roughly four feet and carry fragrant, heavily budded flowers from midseason into late summer, with dependable rebloom. It later received the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award, given annually to the most outstanding eyed or banded cultivar. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring or fall to keep flower counts high.

common_name: Daylily 'Starman's Quest' (Violet-Mauve Spider with Purple Eye)

planting.note: Plant bare-root fans in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; this diploid spider form benefits from a season to settle before peak bloom.

directions: Bred from a Trahlyta x Persian Pattern cross and registered in 1989, this diploid daylily is a narrow-petaled, crispate spider form in violet-mauve with a dark purple eyezone above a green-chartreuse throat. Dormant-foliage scapes reach around 40 inches and carry large blooms with an unusual, twisted petal form typical of spider-type daylilies. Decades after its introduction it was honored with the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award for outstanding eyed and banded cultivars. Divide crowded clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Daylily 'Gavin Petit' (Tangerine with Black Eye and Edge)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for best eyezone contrast and bud count.

directions: Registered in 2004 from a cross built around Awesome Blossom, this fragrant tetraploid daylily bears tangerine-orange petals rimmed with a sharp black eye and matching black picotee edge above a green throat. Semi-evergreen scapes stay compact at around 27 inches and rebloom through midseason with dependable bud counts. It was later recognized with the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award for outstanding eyed or banded cultivars. Divide every three to four years in spring to keep the clump floriferous and the eye pattern crisp.

common_name: Daylily 'Fashion Police' (Pale Yellow with Mahogany-Red Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and evenly moist, well-drained soil; evergreen foliage types benefit from winter mulch in cold zones.

directions: Registered in 2005 by Dan Trimmer from a Spice Hunter x Calling All Angels cross, this tetraploid daylily opens pale yellow with a bold mahogany-red eyezone above a yellow-green throat. Evergreen scapes reach about 34 inches and produce a moderate bud count with reliable midseason rebloom. The cultivar later earned the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award, which honors the most outstanding eyed or banded daylily of the year. In colder zones, protect evergreen foliage with a loose winter mulch and divide crowded fans every few years in spring.

common_name: Daylily 'Celebration of Angels' (Cream with Black-Purple Halo)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; evergreen foliage benefits from mulch protection where winters are harsh.

directions: Introduced in 1999 by Dan Trimmer from a Moonlit Masquerade x Tet. Dragon's Eye cross, this fragrant tetraploid daylily produces cream-colored blooms with a dramatic black-purple halo eyezone above a green throat. Evergreen-foliage scapes stay compact at around 25 inches and bloom early in the season with reliable rebloom and good bud count. It went on to win the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award for the most outstanding eyed or banded cultivar. Divide every few years in spring to maintain strong flowering and eyezone definition.
